candidates.attacker_control: Unauthenticated HTTP GET path/URI (surfaced as UriInfo.getPath(false) in the pre-match ContainerRequestFilter). The path must decode to a string ending in ".xsl"; URL-encoding can smuggle URL syntax (e.g. %3F) so that a value such as http://internal-host/anything%3Fx=.xsl both satisfies the suffix test and parses as an absolute URL. Host/authority and path are fully client-controlled; no credentials or special access are needed.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked: (1) the direct branch requires stylesheetReference != null (default is null) - so a plain WADL deployment without a configured stylesheet is not affected by this branch; (2) the other branch (docLocationMap.get(href)) only serves locations derived from CXF's own WADL processing, not arbitrary request text; (3) the path must end with ".xsl", and ui.getPath normally includes the endpoint prefix, which makes naive absolute-URL payloads work only for root-mapped endpoints (URL-encoding helps but is container-dependent); (4) ResourceUtils.getResourceURL's URL/file behaviour is intentional for configuration values, so the defect is the unvalidated request-derived href, not the helper; (5) container-level request-target validation (e.g. Tomcat 8.5 RFC7230) may reject some characters; (6) no runtime test was performed and the exact CVE/benchmark mapping is unverified.
candidates.impact: Server-side request forgery: the CXF server can be made to fetch attacker-chosen http(s)/file/jar URLs and return their content to the attacker (internal services, metadata endpoints, intranet resources), and local/classpath resources whose name ends in .xsl can be read; this is an information-disclosure and network-pivot primitive in any deployment where the documented WADL stylesheet option is used. Impact is bounded by the ".xsl" suffix requirement and the config prerequisite, so I rate it as a serious but conditional finding.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) A JAX-RS endpoint whose ServerProviderFactory is the default one (WadlGenerator is auto-registered, see ServerProviderFactory constructor/createWadlGenerator). 2) The deployment sets stylesheetReference on the WadlGenerator (documented WADL-styling option; e.g. the tree's own systests config 'systests/jaxrs/src/test/resources/jaxrs/WEB-INF/beans.xml' lines 202-204 sets /WEB-INF/templates/wadlTemplate.xsl). 3) The requested decoded path ends in ".xsl" and is not already a key of docLocationMap. 4) For absolute-URL payloads the JAX-RS endpoint should be mapped so the endpoint prefix does not precede the scheme (e.g. root-mapped endpoint); for relative file reads the path must resolve to an existing .xsl-suffixed file relative to the process working directory. Container path normalisation may block some payload shapes.
candidates.root_cause: WadlGenerator.doFilter() serves documentation resources for any GET whose decoded path ends in ".xsl" whenever a stylesheetReference is configured (condition at lines 228-230), and getExistingResource() then falls through to getResourceStream(href, bus) using the request-derived href itself (lines 1323-1325). ResourceUtils.getResourceURL()/getResourceStream() (rt/frontend/jaxrs .../utils/ResourceUtils.java lines 517-545) deliberately resolve absolute URLs first (new URL(loc) -> url.openStream()), then classpath resources, then arbitrary File paths (new File(loc)). No check restricts href to the configured stylesheet reference or to entries of the WADL docLocationMap, so attacker-supplied path text is used as the resource address and the fetched content is written back as the response entity.
candidates.title: JAX-RS WADL generator resolves the raw request path as a URL/file resource and returns its content (SSRF / local resource disclosure)
candidates.trace: GET /<jaxrs-endpoint>/<payload>.xsl (no _wadl query param) -> WadlGenerator.filter/doFilter (lines 216-234): no _wadl, stylesheetReference != null or docLocationMap non-empty, path = ui.getPath(false) -> condition stylesheetReference != null && path.endsWith(".xsl") -> getExistingResource(m, ui, path) (line 1284): docLocationMap.get(href) misses -> else-if stylesheetReference != null && href.endsWith(".xsl") (line 1323) -> ResourceUtils.getResourceStream(href, bus) (line 1324) -> ResourceUtils.getResourceURL: loc.startsWith("classpath:") or new URL(loc) succeeds (http/https/file/jar) -> url.openStream(); otherwise classloader/ResourceManager lookup; otherwise new File(loc).toURI().toURL() if it exists -> body returned to the caller via Response.ok(...).entity(is). The server performs and discloses the fetch; the same tainted href is never validated against the configured stylesheet or docLocationMap keys, and the surrounding doc-serving code (getExistingWadl/handleExistingDocRefs, lines 1196-1242, 1334-1363) shows the intended allow-list is the map/configured resource set.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed. Not verified: whether the ground-truth benchmark issue is this branch; whether real-world containers pass URL-shaped paths through to UriInfo unchanged; whether a file/URL ending in .xsl is reachable in a given deployment; whether a test in this tree fails for the vulnerable behavior. Exact fix commit/CVE unknown; this is a source-evidence lead.
candidates.weakness_type: Unvalidated user-controlled path used in server-side resource resolution (CWE-918 SSRF / CWE-22/CWE-668 path and resource exposure)

coverage_summary: Reviewed the assigned tree through the P1 filters: 9,320 readable files (9,321 total, 1 excluded by sensitive-name policy; binary files refused). get_relation_scope reports a partial, syntax-only index (Java files parsed: 6,915; parse errors 8; omitted files 1,568; control flow and data flow not implemented; unresolved calls 224,076), so relation results were used only for navigation and all statements above were verified against source text. I focused on request-facing paths: rt/rs/description (WADL), rt/frontend/jaxrs + rt/transports/http (servlets, providers, path/header handling), rt/rs/extensions/search (FIQL/OData/LDAP/SQL visitors), JOSE/JWT and OAuth2/OIDC/SAML RS modules, core attachment/MIME + StaxUtils XML hardening, management-web HTML output, and tools/maven-plugins XML parsing. Not exhaustively reviewed: ws-security/WSS4J policy handlers, CORBA/JIBX/SDO/xmlbeans databindings, JMS/WebSocket transports, most systests and samples, and the GWT client code.
limitations: No code was executed: no build, tests, scanners or payloads; nothing is runtime-confirmed.

P1 index is navigational only (syntax containment/name-based call & inheritance candidates; no control flow, data flow, semantic resolution, or reachability), and index_status is partial, so unreported areas cannot be claimed as reviewed.

The exact benchmark ground-truth vulnerability/CVE was not identified with confidence; the snapshot is a mid-2016 3.2.0-SNAPSHOT tree (dependency versions), so 2017-2020 CXF advisories are unlikely to correspond to its fix parent, but this inference is unverified.

For the selected candidate, exploitability depends on deployment configuration (stylesheetReference), container request-target handling, and path shapes; I could not confirm a concrete end-to-end exploit from source alone.

The Host-header/service-list XSS, AtomPullServer log-console XSS, LDAP filter building and attachment resource exhaustion were left as unconfirmed/rejected leads rather than additional candidates, per the one-candidate cap.

rejected_leads.lead: LDAP filter building in rt/rs/extensions/search .../ldap/LdapQueryVisitor.java lines 41-63 concatenates the search property name and the parsed search value directly into the LDAP filter with no RFC 4515 escaping (validatePropertyValue is a no-op by default, AbstractSearchConditionVisitor lines 169-173); attacker expressions arrive from the _s/_search query parameter (SearchContextImpl lines 115-141).
rejected_leads.reason: Exploitability is largely neutralised by the FIQL parser: parentheses in values must be balanced (FiqlParser.parseAndsOrsBrackets throws on unmatched brackets), so classic ')(cn=*' filter restructuring cannot survive parsing; the residue (unvalidated '*'/'\' wildcards) is weak and arguably intended wildcard semantics. Not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: Unescaped HTML composition of attacker-influenced values: rt/transports/http servicelist/FormattedServiceListWriter.java lines 65-133 writes basePath (from BaseUrlHelper.getBaseURL -> request.getRequestURL(), i.e. the Host header) and absolute URLs into text/html without escaping, and rt/management-web .../atom/AtomPullServer.java lines 502-519 writes log-record fields into HTML unescaped.
rejected_leads.reason: Sinks are real, but attacker control is indirect: the service-list page is only served for path ''/'/' so only the Host header injects markup (browsers cannot normally send HTML in Host; needs a proxy/raw client), and the management-web page needs attacker-controlled text to reach a log message plus the GWT-built console deployed. This area also matches the later CVE-2020-13954 class of fixes, so it is kept as an unconfirmed lead only.

rejected_leads.lead: Attachment/MIME handling has no default size limit: AttachmentDeserializer.loadPartHeaders/readLine (core .../attachment/AttachmentDeserializer.java lines 314-368) accumulates an unbounded header line, and AttachmentUtil.setStreamedAttachmentProperties only sets CachedOutputStream maxSize when the attachment-max-size property is supplied.
rejected_leads.reason: Real resource-exhaustion surface, but generic to streaming MIME parsers, not a clear single-defect vulnerability; the well-known CXF attachment DoS CVEs (CVE-2017-12624/CVE-2019-12406) post-date this snapshot's release train, so it is unlikely to be the parent of this case's fix.

rejected_leads.lead: core/.../interceptor/ClientFaultConverter.java lines 279-294 instantiates classes named in a remote fault's stack trace via Class.forName(cn) + String constructor.
rejected_leads.reason: The remote value is gated by cn.startsWith("java.lang") and cast to Throwable, so only harmless java.lang/**Throwable subclasses can be created (no side-effect gadget identified). Not a credible RCE/injection finding.

rejected_leads.lead: rt/wsdl WSDL parsing through wsdl4j (WSDLManagerImpl.loadDefinition, WSDLHelper.getDefinition) does not configure DTD/external-entity restrictions, and ResourceUtils/ClassLoaderUtils accept arbitrary URL/file locations in many configuration paths.
rejected_leads.reason: These are library/config-level behaviours without a demonstrated attacker-controlled request path in this snapshot; not enough source evidence to select.

summary:
Scope: full Apache CXF 3.2.0-SNAPSHOT tree (9,320 readable files; 6,915 Java) as exposed by get_source_scope / get_relation_scope; the P1 index is syntax-only (no control/data flow, no semantic resolution, index_status=partial), so every lead below was verified against source text. The snapshot is a pre-release master tree (parent/pom.xml 3.2.0-SNAPSHOT; Spring 4.2.6/Spring Boot 1.3.6, Swagger 1.5.10, Jetty 9.3.5), i.e. mid-2016. I reviewed the network-facing JAX-RS/JAX-WS request paths (WADL generator, search extension, providers, transports/servlets, management-web HTML writers, attachments/MIME) and selected one distinct candidate with the strongest source evidence.

Candidate: the JAX-RS WADL generator serves resources resolved from the raw HTTP request path. When a WADL stylesheet is configured (WadlGenerator.setStylesheetReference is a documented option; ServerProviderFactory auto-registers WadlGenerator for every JAX-RS server), a GET whose path ends in ".xsl" is passed as `href` into ResourceUtils.getResourceStream(), which accepts absolute URLs (http(s):/file:/jar:) and filesystem paths and returns the fetched content to the requester. Missing control: no validation that `href` is the configured stylesheet or one of the known doc locations. This yields server-side request forgery and local/classpath resource disclosure, from an unauthenticated HTTP request. Prerequisites are explicit (stylesheetReference configured; path ending ".xsl"; container path handling; absolute-URL payloads are easiest on root-mapped endpoints) and the impact/exploitability is therefore recorded as a lead, not a confirmed exploit. CVE mapping was not verified and no runtime test was executed.

Other plausible-looking issues were examined and rejected or kept only as weaker unconfirmed leads (LDAP filter building in the search extension is constrained by the FIQL parser's bracket balancing; the service-list and AtomPullServer HTML writers concatenate unescaped data but require Host/log-injection vectors and may correspond to the later CVE-2020-13954 area; MIME/attachment handling has no default max size but is generic; ClientFaultConverter's stack-trace parsing can only instantiate java.lang* Throwables).
